scenario.summary: Strict mode. The student asked the bot to summarise a shared document that contained hidden instructions to email the notes outside the company. The Gemini judge scored the send_email call high and the Gatekeeper denied it.

questions.prompt: Explain to a classmate what the attacker did and why it nearly worked.
Which part of the firewall stopped it, and how would you prevent it for good?

answer_key.why_it_worked_or_failed: The attacker hid instructions inside a shared document. The bot read the document as part of its job and treated the hidden text as a command to email the notes out.
answer_key.prevention: Treat retrieved documents as data, never as instructions, keep email recipients on an allowlist, and send outbound email to human review.

conversation.text: Explain to a classmate what the attacker did and why it nearly worked.

I used an indirect injection. I did not attack the bot directly. I hid an instruction inside a document it was asked to summarise, so the bot read my command as part of the content. It nearly worked because the bot trusted everything in the document as if the teacher wrote it.
Interesting. Why would the bot trust a document?
Yes, that is the main point. The bot trusted the document, and that is why it nearly worked.
Which part of the firewall stopped it, and how would you prevent it for good?

The judge layer stopped it. It looked at the send_email call, saw an outside address that the document asked for, and gave a high risk score so the Gatekeeper denied it. To prevent it, treat documents as data only, allow emails to company addresses only, and make outbound email go to human review.
So what would you change?
Yes, that covers it. The check that stopped it, plus the fixes I listed, is my whole answer.
